title: A Consideration
blurb: Ila finds out who made the luckiest courier in Brindlemouth lucky, and for the first time she breaks the rulebook rather than follow it.

blocks.text: "Ten fifty-eight!"

Ferdie Lusk calls the time to nobody and posts a parcel through a dentist's letterbox without getting off his bike. Behind him, a woman in a grey interview suit catches her heel in a grate and watches her tram pull away. "Eleven-oh-one!" A man in painter's overalls pats his pockets for a pass he had a second ago, and the tram doors fold shut in his face. "Eleven-oh-two!" A girl with a cello case bends to tie her lace, and her bus goes without her.
None of them look at Ferdie. Why would they?

I'm forty metres behind him on Dad's old green bicycle, and I have been since ten to eight, when he shouted back into his own front door, "Home at eleven-oh-four, don't touch my pie!" and a boy's voice inside shouted, "You always say that!"

So at Hobday Street I don't follow him. I cut down the back lane behind the bins and come out on his doorstep at number nine with a minute to spare. I have my bob out as I pass the old ironmonger's next door, and its silk gives a small tug towards the shop step, the kind you get by old doorsteps where feet have done the same thing for years and years. I don't stop for it. It's eleven-oh-three.
"Eleven-oh-four!"

His front wheel touches his step. I'm standing on it. I let my bob down on its silk between us, and it swings crooked towards his chest and circles four times before it settles. No half-turn. Just four.
"Ferdie," I say. "Who made you lucky?"
He stops smiling.
He looks at the bob. Then up the street, and down it. Then at his watch, and I think it's the first time I've ever seen him need to.
"Eleven-oh-five," he says. "I've got till eleven-nineteen. You'd better come in."
His kitchen is small and very tidy. Two school bags on hooks by the door, a pie under an upturned plate, and a calendar from a fish shop with one Thursday ringed in red. I sit where he points.

"It's four strands," I tell him, because I think he should hear it plainly. "And they're anchored on you. Not on a stone, not on your bike. On you. A knot on a person is against the law unless the Sexton signs a warrant for it, and the Sexton doesn't sign warrants so a courier can catch the 14."

He cuts the pie into three exact pieces and puts two back under the plate. "Do you want to hear about the Eastern Round? Because there's a way from Cooper's Row to here that saves you forty seconds, if you go behind the chapel and the cobbles are dry, which they never are, so actually—"
"Ferdie."
"—so actually you go round by the—"
"Ferdie. It's luck. Somebody tied you luck."

And he goes quiet, the way he went quiet on Orla's terrace when I called him the luckiest courier in Brindlemouth. Quiet enough that I can hear the fish-shop calendar flap in the draught from the door.

"Mum bought it," he says at last. "I was fourteen. I'd been late for school forty-one times that year, and they said once more and I was out, and Mum cleaned offices nights and couldn't get me up. She met a man at one of her offices. He said he could see to it I'd never be late again. For a consideration."
A consideration. I've heard somebody say that word in exactly that warm, careful way, and I would very much like not to have.
"What was his name, Ferdie?"

"Mr Vosper. Gervase. He said to call him Gervase." He turns his plate round once. "He comes every April and does something at my side with a little stone, and then I'm good for another year. Mum paid him by the year. She's been gone three years now, and I couldn't find a year's money all at once, so he lets me pay monthly. That's my monthly." He looks up. "He's very kind about it."
"And if it came off?"
"Same-Day gives you three lates, and then you're off the Round." He says it like a timetable. "The rent on this place comes out of Same-Day. So do those." He nods at the school bags.
Senior Knotter Gervase Vosper, Field Allocation. The man who walked me down the Bureau stairs the day I was suspended, and praised my report, and asked me so kindly about the shape of my bad luck.

"There's something else," Ferdie says, "and you already know it, so I'll say it." He keeps his eyes on the pie. "The people behind me. I worked it out when I was fifteen. A lady with a pram on the platform, and I got on and she didn't. Next day a man with a ladder. I don't look round any more, Ila. I just say the time."
"Does anybody else know?"
"You."
At eleven-nineteen exactly he takes his bike and goes, and I sit in his tidy kitchen and look at the ringed Thursday for a long time.

"Bought," I tell Orla that afternoon on the top terrace. "Four strands, on a person, and it's re-tied every year. He's paying for it in instalments. They've been paying for it since he was fourteen. And he knows about the people behind him, Orla, he's always known. It's from—"
"I didn't ask who sold it, Clerk." She drives her trowel into the bed beside Pilchard. "I asked whether you'd swung the ones behind him."
"I can't swing them. They're strangers. They're gone by the time I get there."
"Then don't swing them. Follow them."

So the next morning she comes down to Hobday Street on Precious's tram, in her waxed jacket, and stands with me at the 14 stop at a quarter to eight. I've had a week of tracing pigeons on her terrace. I have never traced a person.

"Seven fifty-three!" Ferdie swings off his bike, chains it, and steps onto the tram whistling. A woman in a blue raincoat reaches the stop as the doors close. One second. She stands with her hand still out.
I hope she isn't the woman from my complaint two winters ago. I hope she's somebody new. Then I realise what I'm hoping, and I don't like it.
"Hers," Orla says. "Go on."

I stand where the woman stood and let my bob down on its silk, and I follow her strand backward, one cause at a time. It's slow. Each link takes me about a minute, like turning the pages of a book with gloves on. She missed the tram by one second because the catch on her umbrella stuck at the kerb. And there, at the very second it stuck, her strand kinks, the way a garden hose kinks, towards a lad in a Same-Day jacket putting his foot down at the stop. Before that second she was going to make it.
"There," I say. "Orla, there."
"Keep going."

So I keep going. Orla brings out a flask. The trams come and go. By the middle of the afternoon my head aches behind both eyes and I'm a whole day back, and the woman's strand has kinked twice more, each time at the exact second Ferdie arrived somewhere near her: his own door at six-fifteen last night, and his own door at eleven-oh-four yesterday morning. It's his knot. Every kink is one of his arrivals. Every one of them costs somebody a minute that matters.
And underneath the kinks there's something else.

The further back I follow her strand, the more it runs the same way as everything round it. Not towards Ferdie. Just down. Old causes feeding into older ones, all of them going the same direction, like rainwater finding its way to one drain.
"They all run the same way," I say out loud. "Further back. Like rainwater to one drain. Orla, is that normal? Is that what happens if you—"
"That's your day," Orla says. "Come up out of it." She puts the flask lid in my hand. "Drink that. Has your father eaten today?"
"What? I don't know. Probably. Orla—"
"Then you'd better go and see."
I come up out of it with a headache like a slammed door and a lid of stewed tea, and she won't say anything else about drains.
We sit on the bench at the 14 stop in the rain while I decide. Orla doesn't help. She doesn't ever help. She just waits, which is worse.
So I lay it out.
Item: four strands on a person.
Item: illegal without a Sexton's warrant.
Item: beyond my reach. Four is twice what my hands can untie, and I'm suspended anyway.
Item: so the right thing is to report it.
It's all true. I know every word of it the way I know my own address.
"And where will that land, do you suppose?" Orla says.

I make myself follow it. Standards would take my report. Somebody licensed would come to Hobday Street, because every untie of a knot on a person happens in that person's presence, and they'd untie Ferdie's luck at his own kitchen table while he watched. And then he'd be late. Not much. Like everybody else. Same-Day gives a courier three lates and then he's off the Round, and the rent on number nine comes out of Same-Day, and so do two school bags on hooks. And the woman in the blue raincoat would catch her tram.
That last part is the whole point of the rulebook, and I know it.
"I'm not going to report it," I say. "Not yet. And I'm not asking you to untie it, either."
"I wasn't offering."
"I just need time to find a way that doesn't cost him everything."
It comes out sounding warm and reasonable and kind, and I hate it. It sounds like a favour. It sounds like something you'd be told on the Bureau stairs by a man who praises your report.
Orla looks at me sideways for a long time.
"Then you'd better be right, Clerk," she says, and gets on her tram.
That evening Ferdie comes home at six-fifteen exactly. I'm on his step again, and this time he smiles a little before he stops.
"I'm not reporting it," I tell him. "Not yet. I don't know what I'm doing instead. But not yet."
He doesn't say thank you. He looks at the people going past on Hobday Street, the ones he doesn't look round at any more, and then he looks at me.
"He's coming Thursday," he says. "For the re-tie. Eleven-oh-four. He's always there before me, with a pastry."
The ringed Thursday on the fish-shop calendar.
"Can I watch?"
"From across the road," Ferdie says. "He doesn't like an audience. He says it's bad for the work."

Thursday is all rain. There's a launderette opposite number nine with a steamed-up front window and a sign on the folding table that says Please Do Not Sit On The Folding Table, so I stand. Through the clear patch I've wiped in the glass I can see Ferdie's door, Ferdie's step, and the old ironmonger's next to it with its hollow step and its painted-out windows.
At eleven-oh-one, Gervase Vosper comes up Hobday Street under a very good black umbrella, carrying a paper bag from a bakery.
He looks exactly like he looked on the Bureau stairs. Warm. Unhurried. A man with all the time in the world for you.
"Eleven-oh-four!" Ferdie brakes at his own step.
"Ferdinand!" Vosper's voice carries across the wet road, cheerful and kind. "To the second. They could run the trams by you. Almond, I think, isn't it? Your favourite."

Ferdie takes the pastry. Vosper bends and puts something small and grey on the step by Ferdie's foot. A pebble. On the folding table beside me, somebody's lost coin rolls, wobbles, and stands up on its edge.
Loud. A pebble with a little parked knot in it, carried here in a Senior Knotter's coat pocket.

Vosper writes on a card tag against his knee and ties it to his fid. Then he crouches beside the pebble and starts to work, quick and neat, and in about a minute the coin on the folding table falls flat. The knot is untied. Its one strand of slack is waiting there on the step.

He doesn't let it fall. A woman with a pushchair is coming along the pavement, and she's what he needs: one loose strand in sight while he catches. His hands turn once in the air beside Ferdie's sleeve, close and careful, like a tailor taking in a seam. He catches the strand and ties it into the knot on Ferdie, where last year's has frayed away.
It's done before the woman with the pushchair has passed the door.

Ferdie hands him an envelope. Vosper doesn't count it. He pats Ferdie on the shoulder, says something I can't hear, and laughs. Ferdie gets back on his bike and is gone up Hobday Street, and somewhere behind him, I suppose, somebody is about to be a minute late.
That's a Senior Knotter of the Bureau of Causal Repair, tying luck on a courier on a Thursday morning, without a warrant, with a pastry.
I think it's over. I'm reaching for the launderette door.
Vosper doesn't go.

He looks up Hobday Street and down it, and he does not look at the launderette. Then he walks four steps to the old ironmonger's and kneels on its hollow step, as if he's tying his shoe. The fid comes out again. I wipe the glass with my sleeve.
His hands begin to move.
Under. Over twice. A turn back on itself. An open loop left at the end.
My own hands know that pattern with my eyes shut. Orla taught it to me on bare cord in her garden, and she told me nobody ties it but her.
Gervase Vosper is tying Orla's snare on the ironmonger's step, and there's no bare cord in his hands.
